vocab.def: The amount paid regularly to keep an insurance policy active, whether or not you file a claim
vocab.example: $210 per month for a health plan.

vocab.def: The amount you pay for covered costs before the insurer starts paying
vocab.example: With a $1,000 auto deductible, a $3,200 repair costs you $1,000.

vocab.def: A fixed amount paid for a covered service, such as a doctor visit
Your percent share of covered costs after the deductible is met
vocab.example: 20% of a $4,000 bill after the deductible = $800.

vocab.def: The most you pay for covered care in a plan year; after that, the plan pays 100% of covered costs
vocab.example: A $6,000 maximum caps costs even after a $90,000 surgery.

vocab.def: A formal request to an insurer to pay for a covered loss
vocab.example: Filing a claim after a car accident.

vocab.def: The maximum amount an insurer will pay for a covered loss
The probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes
Many people pay premiums so the losses of the few who have claims can be covered
vocab.example: 1,000 drivers each pay $1,200 so the company can pay the accident claims.

vocab.def: Coverage that pays for injuries or damage you cause to others
vocab.example: Auto liability pays the other driver’s repair bills.

vocab.def: Auto coverage that pays to repair your own car after an accident, minus the deductible
vocab.example: Optional on an older, low-value car.

vocab.def: Auto coverage for non-collision damage such as theft, hail, or hitting a deer
vocab.example: A tree branch falls on a parked car.

vocab.def: Doctors and facilities that have agreed to a health plan’s negotiated prices
vocab.example: Out-of-network visits may cost much more or not count toward the deductible.

vocab.def: A tax-advantaged account paired with an eligible high-deductible health plan to save for medical costs
vocab.example: Depositing $100 per month to cover a future deductible.

vocab.def: Choosing to cover a possible loss with your own savings instead of buying insurance
vocab.example: Skipping collision on a $3,000 car and keeping savings for repairs.

vocab.def: How much financial uncertainty a person can handle; affects deductible and coverage choices
vocab.example: A person with $500 in savings should avoid a $5,000 deductible.

lessons.title: Premiums, Deductibles, and Claims
lessons.hook: Would you pay $15/month to protect a $900 phone? Vote and explain.

notes.body: You pay premiums; when a covered loss happens, the insurer pays above the deductible up to limits.
Higher deductible → lower premium. Choose a deductible your savings can cover.

discussion: Why might someone not file a small claim?
misconceptions: Premiums are refunded if no claims.
reflection: What deductible could you handle today?
lessons.extension: Compare two fictional auto quotes with different deductibles.
lessons.realWorld: Many states require auto liability coverage; lenders require collision on financed cars.

lessons.title: Out-of-Pocket Costs in Health Plans
objectives: Compute out-of-pocket costs with deductibles, coinsurance, copays, and maximums.
Compare total annual costs across plans.
lessons.hook: Two friends with the same $12,000 surgery pay $1,700 and $6,000. How?

notes.body: Pay up to the deductible, then coinsurance, plus copays; stop at the out-of-pocket maximum.
Out-of-network care can cost far more.

discussion: Who might prefer a high-deductible plan?
misconceptions: After the deductible, insurance pays everything.
Show coinsurance continuing to the maximum.
reflection: Which plan would you choose for yourself, and why?
lessons.extension: Use the Decision Lab “Insurance Decision Lab”.

extend: Graph total cost vs. bills for each plan (piecewise functions).

lessons.realWorld: Insurers must provide a standardized Summary of Benefits and Coverage.

lessons.title: Expected Value and Pricing Risk
objectives: Explain how insurers set premiums with risk pooling.
lessons.hook: Game: pay $1 to roll a die; win $5 on a 6. Should you play? Why does the house like this game?

notes.body: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add.
Expected claim cost + expenses and profit.
People buy insurance to avoid ruin, even when EV says they lose a little on average.

discussion: Is buying an extended warranty a good idea? Use EV.
misconceptions: Simulate many years to show variation.
reflection: When is it worth paying more than EV for protection?
lessons.extension: Simulate 100 renters with random claims in a spreadsheet.
lessons.realWorld: Actuaries use probability models to set premiums.

lessons.title: Evaluating Financial Risk and Coverage
objectives: Analyze liability limits and personal exposure.
lessons.hook: Scenario cards: a hailstorm, a slip-and-fall, a stolen bike. Who pays?

notes.body: Liability (others), collision/comprehensive (your car), renters/homeowners (property + liability), health.
Costs above limits can become your personal debt.
Reasonable for small losses if savings can absorb them.

discussion: Why might higher liability limits be worth it?
reflection: Which risks in your life would you insure, and which would you self-insure?
lessons.extension: Research your state’s minimum auto liability limits.

extend: Design a full household insurance plan with a budget.

lessons.realWorld: Umbrella policies add liability coverage above auto and home limits.

questions.prompt: Hana's car is worth about $5,500. Collision coverage costs $720 per year with a $500 deductible. She has $6,000 in savings. Should she keep collision coverage?

parts.prompt: What is the most collision coverage would ever pay on this car?
How many years of premiums equal that maximum payout?
If the chance of a collision claim is about 8% per year, what is the expected yearly payout?
Make a recommendation that considers savings and risk tolerance.

questions.answer: Max payout $5,000; expected payout $400.00 vs premium $720.
questions.modelResponse: Collision would pay at most $5,000, while the expected yearly payout ($400.00) is less than the $720 premium. Because Hana has $6,000 saved — enough to replace the car — self-insuring is reasonable; put the premium savings into the emergency fund.

How many years of premiums equal that maximum payout?
If the chance of a collision claim is about 8% per year, what is the expected yearly payout?
